book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Specialty Fat Stack—What Manorama Actually Sells
question: What exact products does Manorama manufacture, what share of revenue and volume does each contribute, and how does each product solve a real-world problem for named global buyers?

epigraph.quote: In chocolate, a fraction of a degree in melting point is the difference between a crisp snap and a ruined shelf.
epigraph.author: Confectionery Formulation Principle

web_blocks.title: Revenue & Volume Architecture: Value-Added Fats vs. Co-Products

web_blocks.html: Manorama Industries runs one integrated specialty-fats value chain. Yet its commercial output splits into four clear product streams [14, 15]. Specialty fats, exotic butters, and Cocoa Butter Equivalents (CBE) generate ~98.3% of total sales [15]. Within that portfolio, management has steadily shifted the mix toward higher-margin grades. Today, CBE (sold under the MILCOA® brand) and stearin fractions drive 70% to 75% of total revenue, up from 65%–70% earlier [14, 15]. Exotic butters, olein fractions for bakery and personal care, and de-oiled cake (DOC) make up the rest [15].

Analysts must separate revenue share from physical volume share. De-oiled cake is the solid meal left after solvent extraction of sal, mango, and shea kernels. It accounts for about 21.7% of physical product volume [15]. Yet DOC adds only a small single-digit share of revenue because it sells as bulk Indian cattle feed [2, 15]. Even so, selling DOC at positive margins matters. Every rupee earned on DOC lowers the net seed cost for the high-margin fat fractions [2].

web_blocks.title: Concrete End-to-End Examples Across Every Business Segment

web_blocks.html:
1. Cocoa Butter Equivalents (MILCOA® CBE) — Confectionery Example (Ferrero / Mondelēz / Hershey / Barry Callebaut):
The Customer Problem: Pure cocoa butter is the costliest fat in a chocolate bar. West African crop failures pushed cocoa prices to record highs in 2024–2025 [25]. Cocoa butter also melts fast in hot markets like India and the Middle East, causing chalky white fat bloom [17, 19].
The Exact Product & Process: Manorama supplies custom-blended MILCOA® CBE. This fat matches the symmetric POP, POS, and SOS triglycerides of cocoa butter [14, 19]. At Birkoni, Manorama fractionates sal fat, mango fat, and shea butter into hard stearin, refines it, and blends it with palm mid-fraction [14, 19]. Both EU Directive 2000/36/EC and India's FSSAI 2018 rules allow up to 5% CBE in real chocolate [17, 18].
Pricing & Commercials: Contracts use a cost-plus conversion spread rather than spot cocoa bets [19]. CBE realizations held steady around $5,000–$6,000/MT [19]. Once Ferrero, Mondelēz, or Barry Callebaut qualifies a blend over 3 to 5 years, switching costs stay high [14, 19].

2. Exotic Cosmetic & Personal Care Butters — Skincare Example (L'Oréal / The Body Shop):
The Customer Problem: Beauty leaders like L'Oréal and The Body Shop need natural, traceable emollients for lip balms and body butters [14, 21]. Those fats must melt smoothly near skin temperature (~34°C–37°C) and pass strict European clean-beauty audits [14, 21].
The Exact Product & Process: Manorama buys wild West African shea nuts from women's cooperatives and Indian mango or kokum kernels [14, 16]. At Birkoni, it refines, bleaches, and deodorizes the crude butter to remove odor and free fatty acids while keeping natural moisturizers [14, 16].
Pricing & Commercials: Products ship in drums or cartons via Manorama's 30,000 MTPA packing line [5]. Annual contracts price on raw-nut cost plus refining margin and a traceability premium [21].

3. Olein Fractions & Specialty Bakery Fats — Culinary & Spreads Example:
The Customer Problem: Fractionating crude shea or sal fat for hard CBE stearin always creates a softer co-fraction called olein. Leaving olein unsold would hurt plant margins.
The Exact Product & Process: Using its May 2023 interesterification unit at Birkoni, Manorama turns sal and shea olein into trans-fat-free bakery shortenings, pastry margarines, and spread bases [2, 23].
Pricing & Commercials: These fats price against palm olein and hydrogenated oils. That ensures full monetization of every tonne of crude fat processed.

4. De-Oiled Cake (DOC) — Circular By-Product Example (Indian Cattle Feed Mills):
The Customer Problem: Dairy and cattle-feed mills in Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat need low-cost protein and fiber meal for animal rations.
The Exact Product & Process: After Manorama's 90,000 MTPA milling and extraction lines strip 12%–15% oil from sal or mango seeds, the remaining meal becomes de-oiled cake (DOC) [2, 15].
Pricing & Commercials: Manorama sells DOC in bulk bags to local feed mills at domestic feed-parity rates [2, 15]. Though DOC is ~21.7% of physical volume, its role is simple cost recovery on the seed [2, 15].

web_blocks.title: Geographic Revenue Shift: Why Domestic Surged from 27% to 43% in FY26

web_blocks.html: Manorama was long an export-led supplier. In FY25, exports generated 73% of sales while India contributed 27% [2]. In FY26, domestic sales jumped to 43% of revenue, even as exports grew in rupee terms to 57% [2]. Two shifts drove this change. First, global chocolate makers with Indian plants—such as Mondelēz and Ferrero—moved CBE sourcing to Birkoni under India's 5% FSSAI rule to cut import duties and lead times [2, 18]. Second, Indian chocolate and coating brands reformulated recipes faster during the global cocoa price spike [2, 25].

book_paragraphs: To see how Manorama Industries makes money, you and I have to think like chemical engineers at a refinery rather than equity analysts staring at a single revenue line. A wild sal seed or shea nut arriving at Birkoni is not a single product—it is a biological bundle that has to be cracked into four different commercial streams, each with its own customer, pricing logic, and margin profile.

At the top of the value pyramid sits MILCOA, Manorama's flagship Cocoa Butter Equivalent, alongside its core stearin fractions. Together, CBE and stearin generate 70% to 75% of the company's total revenue, up from 65% to 70% a few years ago. Walk into a supermarket in Mumbai, Zurich, or Tokyo and pick up a chocolate bar made by Ferrero, Mondelēz, Hershey, Nestlé, or supplied through industrial giant Barry Callebaut. Under both European Union Directive 2000/36/EC and India's FSSAI regulations, a manufacturer can replace up to 5% of expensive cocoa butter with a specific set of tropical vegetable fats—sal, shea, mango kernel, kokum, illipe, and palm mid-fraction—and still legally sell the bar as pure chocolate.

Why do those multinationals buy MILCOA from Raipur? Partly because cocoa butter prices exploded during the 2024–2025 West African crop crisis, and partly because pure cocoa butter has a glaring physical flaw in hot climates: it melts too easily and blooms white on warm retail shelves. By blending fractionated sal and shea stearin from Birkoni, chocolatiers raise the melting point slightly, preserve the crisp snap, and lock in a cost-plus supply contract around $5,000 to $6,000 per metric tonne. Once a giant like Ferrero or Mondelēz spends three to five years testing your fat on its commercial tempering lines, it does not switch suppliers to save a few dollars a tonne.

book_subsections.title: Beauty Butters: The Clean-Label Emollient Stream
paragraphs: If CBE is the star of the confectionery world, Manorama's second stream—exotic cosmetic and personal care butters—serves an equally demanding buyer: global beauty brands like L'Oréal and The Body Shop. When a formulator designs a lip balm, hair mask, or body butter, she needs a natural fat that stays solid in a jar yet melts cleanly at human skin temperature around 35°C, without synthetic stabilizers.

Crude shea or mango butter straight out of a forest press smells smoky and looks dark brown. At Birkoni, Manorama puts that crude butter through physical and chemical refining, bleaching, and deodorization to strip out free fatty acids and odor while preserving natural moisturizing unsaponifiables. Crucially, European beauty buyers also audit the social trail: Manorama backs its shipments with direct procurement records from West African women's cooperatives and packs finished drums on its 30,000 MTPA packing line, earning a traceability premium on top of its refining spread.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Look at the FY26 geographic shift: domestic revenue jumped from 27% in FY25 to 43% in FY26. That tells you global FMCG giants aren't just buying from Manorama for Europe—they are qualifying Birkoni to supply their massive Indian chocolate factories directly, cutting freight and import friction.

book_subsections.title: Olein Co-Fractions and De-Oiled Cake: Balancing the Mass Equation
paragraphs: Every time a solvent fractionator isolates hard stearin for chocolate, it simultaneously produces liquid olein. If you couldn't sell the olein, your plant economics would collapse. Using the interesterification unit commissioned at Birkoni in May 2023, Manorama converts sal and shea olein into trans-fat-free bakery shortenings, puff-pastry fats, and chocolate-spread bases for food-service clients.

And what about the solid seed meal left behind after hexane strips out the 12% to 15% oil content? That becomes de-oiled cake. While de-oiled cake represents roughly 21.7% of Manorama's physical tonnage, it contributes only a minor share of revenue, sold in bulk bags to Indian cattle-feed mills across Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, and Gujarat. Its job is not to drive headline growth—it is to turn extraction residue into steady domestic cash that lowers the net cost of every seed entering the gate.

Put all four streams together and you see why Manorama's business model is so resilient when run at high utilization: the same seed funds cattle feed at the bottom, bakery oleins in the middle, and high-margin CBE and cosmetic butters at the top.

book_subsections.title: Walkthrough: Inside a European Chocolate Line & a Cosmetic Jar
paragraphs: To see why a multinational confectioner pays Manorama a specialty margin instead of buying commodity palm oil, walk with me onto a European chocolate molding line. A global chocolatier like Ferrero or Mondelez needs a fat phase that stays rock-solid at room temperature—giving a crisp snap when you break a bar—yet melts sharply between 32°C and 35°C on the human tongue without leaving a waxy film. Pure cocoa butter does this naturally, but West African cocoa harvests swing wildly with El Niño weather and swollen-shoot tree disease. Under European Union and FSSAI rules, manufacturers can replace up to 5% of cocoa butter with Cocoa Butter Equivalents made from non-lauric exotic fats—specifically sal, shea, mango kernel, and kokum stearin blended with palm mid-fraction.

Manorama does not sell a generic drum of oil into that factory. Its chemists in Birkoni fractionate crude sal and shea fats into high-purity symmetrical triglycerides—principally 1,3-distearoyl-2-oleoyl-glycerol, or SOS—whose crystallization curve mirrors cocoa butter down to the tenth of a degree. Once a customer's R&D lab validates that curve across shelf-life, bloom-resistance, and sensory taste tests over three to five years, switching suppliers risks ruining millions of chocolate bars. That is why value-added CBE and stearin climbed to roughly 75% of Manorama's sales value in H1 FY27.

Now step across to the personal-care aisle. A natural-cosmetics formulator needs refined shea butter and mango butter with ultra-low free fatty acids, zero off-odor, and consistent slip for lip balms, body lotions, and hair masks. By taking the olein and refined butter fractions left over from CBE stearin separation, Manorama monetizes both halves of every nut it crushes—turning what would otherwise be a low-value by-product into a second high-margin revenue stream.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: When a company sells the stearin fraction to chocolate makers and the olein/butter fraction to personal-care brands—while selling the residual de-oiled cake to animal feed—every kilogram of forest seed generates layered margin instead of waste.

book_subsections.title: Domestic vs. Export Mix: Why Indian Confectioners Are Catching Up
paragraphs: Look closely at Manorama's geographic mix shift between FY25 and H1 FY27, because it reveals a quiet second growth engine. In FY25, exports accounted for 73% of revenue and domestic Indian sales just 27%. By FY26, domestic share climbed to 43% against 57% exports on a much larger ₹1,367 crore base—and in H1 FY27, exports stood at roughly 61% as global orders surged 40.8% year-on-year.

Why are both domestic and export lines firing together? In India, rising cocoa prices and expanding modern-retail chocolate consumption have pushed both multinational subsidiaries and domestic confectionery brands to reformulate coatings, spreads, and compound chocolates using FSSAI-compliant CBEs and specialty stearins. Meanwhile, overseas buyers in Europe, Latin America, and Asia continue qualifying Birkoni's expanded fractionation lines to diversify away from single-region West African supply bottlenecks.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Never confuse physical tonnage with profit drivers in an extraction business. De-oiled cake is over a fifth of Manorama's volume, yet the entire investment thesis rests on the 70%–75% of revenue coming from fractionated CBE and stearin.
